sections.title: Cold open
notes: The whole film is built on one idea: the Wolfram Language told as a natural language, gaining words. So it opens on the thesis, typed.
The melody under it is Rule 30: the centre column of CellularAutomaton[30] picks notes from an A-minor pentatonic scale. The same melody returns alone at the very end.

sections.title: SMP, 1979–81
notes: SMP started in November 1979 at Caltech; Wolfram was 20. The session uses SMP’s real prompt format, #I[n]:: for input and #O[n]: for output.

Graph[Sin[1/x],x,0.02,0.2] is the example from the SMP Reference Manual §10.2, and the character plot follows the manual’s style: stars joined into vertical runs, tick values written into the underscore axis.
The pinned print is the real SMP manual cover from July 1981.

sections.title: Mathematica 1.0, June 23, 1988
captions: Its first vocabulary: 554 words.
Words for pictures, too.
notes: The window is Mac System 6, rendered at half resolution and thresholded to one bit. Only pictures are dithered, so text stays crisp. The menus are the 1.0 menus: File, Edit, Cells, Search, Action, Styles, Windows.

Labels sit above cells in italics, input is bold Courier, graphics print -SurfaceGraphics-: all 1988 conventions. Integrate’s answer is shown in 1.0’s two-dimensional character layout, because typeset output only arrived in 3.0.
The counter starts at 554: the documented words introduced in 1.0, from WolframLanguageData. Every one of them flies onto the wall behind the window.

sections.title: NeXT, 1988
captions: Bundled with every NeXT computer. And Spikey is born.
notes: Mathematica shipped with every NeXT computer. The window uses NeXTSTEP’s four greys, the vertical menu and the scroller on the left.

Spikey is born here: <<Polyhedra.m, then Show[Graphics3D[Stellate[Icosahedron[]]]], exactly as in the archive scan. Today’s Stellate returned a plain icosahedron, so the stellation was rebuilt the way the 1.0 package did it, with each apex at twice the face centroid.

snippets.code:
With[{v = PolyhedronData["Icosahedron", "VertexCoordinates"]},
 Graphics3D[{GrayLevel[0.8], Polygon[Flatten[Table[{#1, #2, 2 Mean[v[[f]]]} & @@@ Partition[v[[f]], 2, 1, 1], {f, PolyhedronData["Icosahedron", "FaceIndices"]}], 1]]}]]
snippets.label: Spikey’s birth, rebuilt without the 1.0 Polyhedra package: each face raised to twice its centroid

sections.title: Mathematica 2.0, January 1991
captions: It learns to make sound, and to draw in colour.
notes: Version 2 gave the language sound. The waveform is drawn from the kernel’s own samples of Play[Sin[1000 t (1 + t)] Sin[2 Pi t], {t, 0, 1.5}], and that exact sound is mixed into the soundtrack at the moment the cell evaluates.
Windows 3.1 chrome, pure-blue cell brackets and the “Bytes Free” status bar come from real 2.x screenshots.

sections.title: Mathematica 6.0, May 2007
captions: It learns about the world.
And about computation itself.
And it starts to answer back.
notes: Curated data (WordData, CountryData), TuringMachine and Manipulate are all 6.0. The Europe map is drawn from CountryData polygons, not GeoGraphics, which is 10.0.

The Manipulate slider also drives the soundtrack: its value sets the music’s low-pass filter. When the slider settles at a = 1.8, the mouse rotates the surface, because 6.0 is when 3D graphics became rotatable by mouse.

snippets.code:
Graphics[{EdgeForm[White], ColorData["SunsetColors"][1 - Rescale[Log[QuantityMagnitude[CountryData[#, "Population"]]], {11, 18.5}]],
    CountryData[#, "Polygon"] /. GeoPosition[p_] :> Reverse /@ p} & /@ CountryData["Europe"],
 PlotRange -> {{-25, 45}, {34, 72}}]
snippets.label: In[2]: Europe by population (today’s CountryData polygons are geo positions, hence the conversion)

sections.title: Mathematica 7, November 2008
captions: It learns to work in parallel.
notes: Built-in parallel computing: the Julia set was computed with ParallelTable across 16 kernels, and each colour stripe marks the rows one kernel actually computed ($KernelID).

snippets.code:
julia = Compile[{{z0, _Complex}}, Module[{z = z0, n = 0}, While[Abs[z] < 2 && n < 120, z = z^2 + (-0.8 + 0.156 I); n++]; n]];
Colorize[Image[Rescale[Log[1. + ParallelTable[julia[x + I y], {y, 0.95, -0.95, -0.0064}, {x, -1.6, 1.6, 0.0067}]]]], ColorFunction -> "SunsetColors"]
snippets.label: In[5]: a Julia set, rows computed in parallel

sections.title: Mathematica 8, November 2010
captions: It learns to understand English.
It learns graphs: countries, linked by their borders.
notes: Free-form input turned plain English into code. Graph arrived in 8.0; the network is Europe’s borders from CountryData, laid out by longitude and latitude.

snippets.label: What the free-form query “countries in europe” turns into

snippets.code:
With[{eu = CountryData["Europe"]},
 Graph[DeleteDuplicates[Sort /@ Flatten[Table[UndirectedEdge[c, #] & /@ Intersection[CountryData[c, "BorderingCountries"], eu], {c, eu}]]],
  VertexLabels -> Automatic]]
snippets.label: In[7]: Europe’s borders as a Graph

sections.title: The Wolfram Language, 2013–14
captions: Version 10 adds 1,022 words: the most ever.
The Earth, the stars, every country and language.
It even knows about its own words.
notes: Named in November 2013 and free on every Raspberry Pi. Version 10 added 1,022 words, the largest single release.
The globe’s night side is computed for 9 July 2014 at 12:00 UTC, the 10.0 release date, with great circles from Champaign. The star plot is StarData for the naked-eye stars.
The last graph is the language describing itself: 186 words linked by WolframLanguageData’s RelatedSymbols. That function is 10.2, so the era label changes to 10.2 for it.

snippets.code:
With[{home = Entity["City", {"Champaign", "Illinois", "UnitedStates"}],
   cities = {Entity["City", {"London", "GreaterLondon", "UnitedKingdom"}], Entity["City", {"Tokyo", "Tokyo", "Japan"}], Entity["City", {"SaoPaulo", "SaoPaulo", "Brazil"}], Entity["City", {"Sydney", "NewSouthWales", "Australia"}]}},
 GeoGraphics[{GeoStyling[Opacity[0.5]], NightHemisphere[DateObject[{2014, 7, 9, 12}, TimeZone -> 0]], Red, GeoPath[{home, #}, "GreatCircle"] & /@ cities},
  GeoProjection -> "Orthographic", GeoRange -> "World"]]
snippets.label: In[2]: night side on the 10.0 release date, great circles from Champaign
In[4]: the naked-eye stars, temperature against brightness

snippets.code:
With[{seeds = {"List", "Plot", "Map", "Graph", "Entity", "Image", "Manipulate", "GeoGraphics"}},
 Graph[DeleteDuplicates[Sort /@ Flatten[Table[UndirectedEdge[s, CommonName[#]] & /@ Take[WolframLanguageData[s, "RelatedSymbols"], UpTo[8]], {s, seeds}]]],
  VertexLabels -> Automatic]]
snippets.label: In[5]: the language’s own words, linked by related symbols

sections.title: Version 12, 2019
captions: Compiled, it runs fast.
Molecules, machines, whole systems.
notes: The FunctionCompile race was measured on the machine that rendered the film: 2.01 s evaluated vs 14.8 ms compiled, the same result both ways.
The double pendulum is a real SystemModelSimulate of the Modelica MultiBody example (SystemModel is 11.3), animated from the simulated positions.

snippets.code:
cf = FunctionCompile[Function[Typed[n, "MachineInteger"], Module[{s = 0., i = 1}, While[i <= n, s += Sin[N[i]]^2; i++]; s]]];
AbsoluteTiming[cf[3*10^6]]
snippets.label: In[4]: compiled (compare with the same loop evaluated)

sections.title: Version 14, 2024–25
captions: It keeps a record of itself.
Its fastest-growing stretch: 53.8 new words a month.
notes: Dark mode arrived in 14.3. The Tabular is real and typed: dates, integers, a characters-unit quantity, months, Entity chips. TransformColumns derives words per month, with the unit carried through automatically.

snippets.code:
versions = Tabular[{
   <|"version" -> "8.0", "released" -> DateObject[{2010, 11, 15}], "new words" -> 638, "since previous" -> Quantity[24, "Months"]|>,
   <|"version" -> "10.0", "released" -> DateObject[{2014, 7, 9}], "new words" -> 1022, "since previous" -> Quantity[19, "Months"]|>,
   <|"version" -> "12.0", "released" -> DateObject[{2019, 4, 16}], "new words" -> 793, "since previous" -> Quantity[32, "Months"]|>}]
snippets.label: In[1]: a typed Tabular (a few rows of the film’s table)

snippets.code: TakeLargestBy[TransformColumns[versions, "words per month" -> Function[Round[#["new words"]/#["since previous"], 0.1]]], "words per month", 3]
